sharing the good news” today we celebrate mission sunday. as we give thanks for the tremendous work of irish missionaries throughout the world, it’s also a good opportunity for us all to reflect on our own mission in the church. st francis of assisi once wrote that in preaching we should use words if necessary. there was never a time when the example of a good christian life was more needed in order to inspire other people. we can certainly underestimate the value of our example and kindness to others. and this is before we open our mouths at all!st paul tells us that: “faith comes from what is heard and what is heard comes through the word of christ.” when speaking about mission st john bosco, who founded the salesians, once said: “never say'it's not my turn' but rather'i'm going'!” i think there may always be a good reason not to do something, not to accept a challenge. but here st john bosco is encouraging us to be generous and courageous. we may not be talking about a radical change in our lifestyle or a move to another country but it may just be that we see a gap somewhere and realise that we can fill it. archbishop dermot farrell, reminds us that one of the great blessings of pope francis’ ministry has been a renewed appreciation of the role of laity. he said, “in our parishes today, through those involved in parish councils, finance committees, liturgy groups, ministers of word and sacrament, and those in so many voluntary roles, the holy spirit continues to pour out gifts for the arrival of god’s kingdom.” we should all reflect on our own mission and ministry as we all have one. our new saint john henry newman once said that we are led to think that we ought to be useful on a large scale and to move away from our usual “line of life”. but he tells us that this should not be the case. “we need not give up our usual manner of life, in order to serve god and that “that the most humble and quietest station is acceptable to him, if improved duly.” there are many things that we can do. newman also wrote about the vocation of saint matthias who was elected by the remaining eleven apostles to replace judas. he said: “we take the place of others who have gone before, as matthias did; filling up the ranks of soldiers, some of whom, indeed, have fought a good fight, but many of whom in every age have made void their calling. many are called, few are chosen.” pope francis said: “it is necessary to recognise “those laymen and women who feel called by virtue of their baptism to cooperate in the work of catechesis.” as pope benedict xvi said, the laity and clergy are “co - responsible” for sharing the good news. it’s a task we all must take on together. our mission now is to reach out beyond our comfort zones and to connect to those who, as st paul said, may never hear the word of god unless we bring it to them ourselves. deacon gerard october and world mission sunday is a time for the faithful of the world to show their from the deacon’s desk this sunday’s gospel giving to god what belongs to god matthew 22:15-21 in this sunday’s gospel, jesus is confronted with a question designed to trap him: should taxes be paid to caesar? his response is both simple and profound: “give back to caesar what belongs to caesar, and to god what belongs to god.” jesus acknowledges our responsibilities as citizens and members of society. we have duties towards the communities in which we live and work. yet he reminds us that there is a deeper loyalty that comes before all others. while coins may bear the image of caesar, each human person bears the image of god. the gospel challenges us to reflect on what belongs to god in our own lives. our time, talents, relationships, compassion, and faith are gifts entrusted to us by the lord. as we fulfil our earthly responsibilities, we are also called to offer ourselves wholeheartedly to god, allowing his values of justice, truth, mercy, and love to shape everything we do. may we live as faithful citizens of the world, while never forgetting that we belong first to god. deacon eric thank you to fr kevin when fr kevin announced in may that he had been appointed by archbishop farrell to a new ministry in wicklow, our church was about to close for essential refurbishment works. as a result, there was little opportunity for parishioners to express their thanks for his seven and a half years of devoted service to our parish. the parish pastoral council recently discussed how we might show our appreciation for fr kevin and agreed to organise a parish collection towards a 18th october 2026 29th sunday in ordinary time render unto god …. when jesus ascended into heaven, as we celebrate on the feast of the ascension, you may remember the angels then appearing to the disciples and asking them – “why are you men from galilee standing here looking into the sky?” it was a natural enough reaction on their part – the jesus whose company they had shared over the previous three years or so, was suddenly gone. their looking into the sky was basically a version of “what next?” many people in our parish over the last couple of weeks have expressed similar feelings of “what next?” – “where do we go from here?” our passi onist superiors, who have the task of stafïng our parish, i’m sure are also feeling something similar. unti l they get things sorted out, they’ve asked me to take temporary responsibility for us providing the best service we can, in the circumstances, for our parishioners – and all who form the greater mount argus community. in such situations i tend to look for hopeful signs in whatever is happening at the moment. and our gospel reading today doesn’t let me down! it’s that passage which ends with the famous saying “give back to caesar what belongs to caesar – and to god what belongs to god”. it comes at the end of a passage in which his opponents have tried to trip up jesus with a question about taxes to the romans. but he has reversed the trap, by getting them to produce a coin with caesar’s image on it – something they should never have had, as any one of them that remembered the story of the golden calf, and the ban on carrying images, would have fully understood. their hypocrisy wouldn’t allow them to acknowledge that they knew, as well as jesus did, that “giving to god” and “giving to caesar” were not two different coins, as it were, but were two sides of the one coin. and that’s the challenge in today’s gospel - the recognition that there are no areas of life that are irrelevant to our relationship with god. it can be easy nowadays to get caugh t up in political discussions on the state of society; the colossal abuse of power and wealth; and what governments masses at mount argus sunday: 8.00 am, 11.00 am, 4.00 pm monday to friday: 10.00 am, 6.15 pm saturdays: 11.00 am, 6.15 (vigil mass) working holydays 6.15 pm vigil, 10.00 am, 6.15 pm church opening hours sunday: 7.30 am to 5.00 pm monday to friday: 9.30 am to 6.45 pm saturday: 10.30 am to 7.00 pm blessing with the relic of st charles monday to friday after 10.00 am mass wednesday, thursday, friday at 4.00 pm saturday after 11.00 am mass sunday after 11.00 am and 4.00 pm mass st charles novena mass: saturday, 11.00 am sacrament of reconciliation wednesday, thursday, friday: 11.00 - 11.30 am, 4.00 - 4.30 pm saturday: 4.00 to 5.30 pm eucharistic adoration wednesdays and fridays: 4.00 to 6.00 pm mount argus

belonging can sound heavy - as if we are being controlled, or our money belongs to us and we can do what we like with it. but for jesus it's the belonging of love, not of power and control. much is not in our control. we are born and die at god's time. this reminds us that we are not the masters of our lives, we come from god and go to god. this belonging is the centre of our human family and community. god doesn't want to control us but to love us. but there's an addition: belonging to god means belonging to each other. we have rights and duties of love. to give to others what belongs to others; give to the poor what belongs to the poor. everyone has a right to the food of the earth and the food of the mind, and shelter for the body. it's not charity when people are given food, education, a home, freedom of religion, freedom of speech - it is justice. to give to god what belongs to god is to share the goods of the earth! think of a time when you made a decision for the common good - money given away, cleaning the neighbourhood, joining a parents' group etc. remember and be grateful lord, may your will that we share well the goods of the world be done. baptism st benedict’s church we welcome kalendra dolores murphy into our community of st benedict’s and keep her and her family in our prayers. edenmore (grange park)

telephone: 01 - 4522251 the wild swans at coole by william butler yeats (1916) the trees are in their autumn beauty, the woodland paths are dry, under the october twilight the water mirrors a still sky; upon the brimming water among the stones are nine-and-fifty swans. the nineteenth autumn has come upon me since i first made my count; i saw, before i had well finished, all suddenly mount and scatter wheeling in great broken rings upon their clamorous wings. i have looked upon those brilliant creatures, and now my heart is sore. all's changed since i, hearing at twilight, the first time on this shore, the bell-beat of their wings above my head, trod with a lighter tread. unwearied still, lover by lover, they paddle in the cold companionable streams or climb the air; their hearts have not grown old; passion or conquest, wander where they will, attend upon them still. but now they drift on the still water, mysterious, beautiful; among what rushes will they build, by what lake's edge or pool delight men's eyes when i awake some day to find they have flown away? understanding the mass. the offertory: "blessed are you, lord god of all creation" what the priest is doing the liturgy of the word is complete. now the altar is prepared, gifts are brought forward, and the mass moves into its second great movement - the liturgy of the eucharist. the priest receives bread and wine, lifts each slightly, and offers quiet prayers of blessing drawn from ancient jewish table prayers. he says these prayers in a quiet voice, or even silently. these are humble gifts, bread and wine, fruit of the earth, work of human hands. but that ordinariness is precisely the point. god does not ask for the extraordinary. he takes what we bring and transforms it entirely. how we should respond the collection taken up at this moment is not an interruption, it belongs here. money represents our labour, our time, our life. placing it in the bags is a small but genuine act of offering ourselves alongside the bread and wine. as the gifts are brought forward, make an interior offering of your own. whatever you are carrying this week work, worry, joy, grief - place it consciously on that altar alongside the bread and wine. living this at mass the offertory is easily overlooked as a moment of transition. reclaim it. when the priest lifts the bread, lift something of yourself with it. pope leoxiv prayer for the recovery of pope leo. loving and merciful god, we pray for our holy father, pope leo, asking you to bless him with healing, strength, and renewed health. be close to him in his time of need, grant him peace and comfort, and guide those who care for him. may he experience your loving presence and be restored to good health, so that he may continue to shepherd your church with wisdom and love. amen. masses 10 am monday to saturday, vigil mass saturday 6.30 pm sunday masses 9 am, 10.30 am, 12 noon . confessions after 10 am mass on saturday and on request baptisms on the 2nd saturday of each month at 2 pm. please contact the parish office contacts parish office 8316016 fr michael o’grady

(birthday remembrance). may they rest in peace. mission sunday. world mission sunday, which is celebrated on the 2nd last sunday of october each year, is the one sunday of the year when the entire global church comes together in support of mission. it is the holy father's annual appeal for spiritual and financial support so that the life giving work of overseas mission and missionaries can continue. mission sunday collections will take place in every single parish where the church is present. it is a moment of universal solidarity when each member of the church family, regardless of location or background, plays their part in supporting each other. all offerings and donations made on world mission sunday become part of the holy father's universal solidarity fund. this fund is a lifeline for struggling missionaries and the communities they serve across africa, asia and latin america, where over 1,100 mission dioceses are found. these dioceses are often in remote areas devastated by war and natural disasters or where suppressed communities are just opening up to the life-saving message of jesus christ. as these dioceses form and grow, so do their needs. the mission
